papers.title: Gene-level evolutionary conservation and human constraint decline at comparable rates across the age of onset of Mendelian disease
papers.abstract: Background Gene-level constraint and conservation scores are widely used to prioritise disease genes and to benchmark genomic language models. Purifying selection acts weakly on phenotypes manifesting after reproduction, so these scores are expected to carry less information about late-onset disease. An onset-dependent gradient has been demonstrated for human allele frequencies but not for the gene-level scores used in practice. Results We built an age-of-onset axis for 2,885 Mendelian diseases from Orphanet and fitted cross-species conservation (241-way phyloP) and human-population constraint (shet) on the same 5,322 gene-disease pairs against matched controls, to test whether one decays faster with onset. Their onset slopes differed by 0.23 logit units (97.5% confidence interval -0.10 to 0.56), equivalent to 0.024 units of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) in a design resolving 0.049; the interval excludes constraint losing discriminative power faster than conservation by more than 0.011 AUROC units, widening to 0.033 when somatic associations are dropped. The usual explanation, that early-onset disease genes are developmental, pleiotropic and haploinsufficient by construction, did not account for the contrast; conditioning barely moved it. The answer did, however, depend on the constraint metric: three alternatives yielded larger contrasts excluding zero, though paired comparison could not distinguish the estimates. The metrics also diverged on recessive disease genes, with shet ranked below the gene pool (AUROC 0.487) and loss-of-function depletion above it (0.533), though, against matched controls, both ranked them below (0.457 and 0.450). Evolutionary scores improved a non-evolutionary baseline by 17 to 23%, with no onset gradient. Conclusions Conservation and constraint do not lose their value at measurably different rates as disease onset rises, and with only 283 late-onset Mendelian diseases annotated genome-wide, the question cannot be settled more finely. The gene-class explanation does not account for the contrast. Metrics that rank genes near-identically can still yield opposite onset-stratified answers, so a result reported by one metric carries a sensitivity that its confidence interval does not show. No constraint metric identifies recessive disease genes against matched controls, so a pipeline with recessive disease in scope needs a correction that switching metric does not supply.

papers.title: A frameshift mutation in PRICKLE1 causes skeletal dysplasia in Cheviot sheep
papers.abstract: Skeletal dysplasias can occur in animals, including humans, and are attributed to both environmental and genetic causes. As our understanding of the distinguishing phenotypes of different skeletal dysplasias improves, alongside elucidation of the mechanisms and genetic networks that contribute to skeletal development, identifying and controlling genetic mutations in livestock populations has become increasingly possible, including approaches beyond selective breeding alone. Within Scotland an 'achondroplasia' syndrome that was first described in the South Country Cheviot breed of sheep (OMIA 000004-9940), has continued to occur periodically within the same geographical locations, despite culling of affected lambs over many decades. Affected lambs exhibit rounded heads, short legs, a loss of hooves, abnormal stance and short twisted tails. As the condition has been observed in flocks and as progeny from specific ram and ewe matings, and cases have been co-twinned to normal siblings, this suggests a syndrome caused by a recessive genetic condition rather than environmental factors. Through homozygosity mapping and whole genome sequence analyses, we identified a 10 bp deletion in the open reading frame of the PRICKLE1 gene that encodes prickle planar cell polarity protein 1 and is essential for normal vertebrate embryonic development. We identified additional phenotypes present in affected lambs, including a loss of phalanges, neural tube defects, vertebral and articular chondrocyte defects, hair orientation differences and polycystic kidneys, consistent with a loss of PRICKLE1 function based on comparisons to mouse mutant lines. These findings enabled the development of a simple DNA test for the identified PRICKLE1 mutation that was made commercially available to facilitate the elimination of this genetic disease from sheep flocks.

papers.title: The replication checkpoint couples fork progression to the release of transcribed genes from nuclear pores
papers.abstract: The nuclear envelope contributes to chromatin compartmentalization in eukaryotes by anchoring heterochromatin to the lamina and active transcription sites to nuclear pore complexes (NPCs). During DNA replication, chromatin association with the nuclear envelope is thought to act as a topological barrier to DNA polymerases, potentially exacerbating transcription-replication conflicts (TRCs). While limited evidence suggests that the DNA replication checkpoint kinase Rad53/CHK1 promotes the release of genes from the NPC during replicative stress, the global scale and precise regulation of this process remain unknown. Through a candidate-based screen, we demonstrate that gene release from NPCs is a general feature of the cellular response to replication stress, tightly coordinated with replication fork progression. We show that the checkpoint kinases Mec1/ATR and Rad53/CHK1 are both essential for managing gene association with NPCs, but operate in a distinct, stepwise manner: Mec1/ATR triggers the initial dissociation by promoting the removal of RNAPII from the DNA, while Rad53/CHK1 prevents the premature reassociation of transcribed loci by phosphorylating the nucleoporin Mlp1. Finally, we demonstrate that maintaining this control over genes-NPC association is critical for efficient DNA replication under stress. Collectively, our findings reveal that the DNA replication checkpoint integrates genome duplication with chromosome spatial positioning to maintain genome integrity during replication stress.

papers.title: Ethanol stress induces siRNA-mediated epimutations and phenotypic variability in fission yeast
papers.abstract: Epigenetic information is required for the maintenance of gene expression states through cell division. Some epigenetic information can also persist through generations, raising the possibility that epigenetic differences may arise in populations and contribute to evolutionary processes such as drift and natural selection. Evaluating this requires characterising the properties of such epimutations, so that their rate, stability and genome-wide distribution can be assessed. Recent experiments in many organisms have demonstrated that epimutations occur, but have limited stability relative to DNA sequence mutations. However, the extent to which epimutations contribute to evolution is still unclear, in part because it is not clear whether epimutations respond dynamically to environmental conditions. Here, we use the fission yeast S. pombe, in which evolutionarily relevant epimutations have been observed, but not yet systematically characterised, to test whether a physiologically relevant stress, ethanol exposure, leads to changes in the properties of epimutations. Using laboratory evolution experiments with repeated population bottlenecks to minimise selection, we show that epimutations associated with changes in small interfering (si)RNAs occur at a greater rate in ethanol. Ethanol-induced epimutations are enriched at transposable element loci and correlate with changes in transposon expression. Ethanol exposure also increases gene expression noise genome-wide and variability in growth rate; importantly, both these increases are suppressed in mutants lacking siRNAs. Together, these results demonstrate that stress can alter the generation of heritable epigenetic information, and suggest that siRNAs may have a role in promoting phenotypic variability in response to environmental stress.

papers.title: Niche-dependent epistasis within the cancer genome shapes metastatic fitness
papers.abstract: Epistasis, the genetic interaction between loci, directs non-additive genotype-to-phenotype outcomes. Within a multicellular organism, how the tissue niche (E) shapes gene-by-gene epistasis (GxG) and its phenotypic consequences remains poorly studied. Using tumor lung metastasis as an experimental model, we mapped GxGxE through combinatorial CRISPR perturbation coupled with depletion of defined host myeloid populations in mice. The metastatic niche first selects disseminated tumor cells on GxG epistatic fitness, then drives transcriptome convergence regardless of genotype. Removing anatomically distinct myeloid populations reshaped the metastatic epistasis landscape despite identical tumor genotypes. Gene-by-gene-by-environment epistasis therefore operates at the organismal level, with interaction magnitude and sign set by niche cells. Beyond metastasis, our data suggest that the tissue niche conditions how genetic interactions translate into divergent phenotypes.

papers.title: Contextualizing the polygenic basis of human brain shape
papers.abstract: As the most recently evolved neuroanatomical trait of our species, our globular head shape ('globularity') constitutes a promising point of entry to probe possible associations between brain morphology and cognitive traits that may be distinctive of Homo sapiens. To shed additional light on the underlying biology of globularity and its cognitive consequences, we capitalize on data pairing genetic variation to brain shape differences from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of 34,595 adults of European ancestry, and embed genome-wide associations of globularity within genetic variation underpinning up to 75 brain-related traits. Through extensive hypergeometric tests, we observe significant associations between globularity and white matter traits at the gene level, but stronger associations with cerebellar volume, ventricular size, and the fornix at the genomic variant level. Combining conjunctional false discovery rate (FDR) with genetic correlations, we notice homogeneously concordant relations between globularity and the volume of the brain ventricles, and homogeneously discordant relations with glymphatic function. We also unravel more selective, spatially organized relations between globularity and cerebellar volume, white matter connectivity and sulcal width. Spatial permutation tests reveal that sulcal width associations are systematically distributed along a sensorimotor-association gradient of cortical organization. Additionally, correlations of brain- and lifespan-wise gene expression patterns linked to globularity and the brain ventricles highlight recurrent associations with the pentose phosphate metabolic pathway. Finally, deploying an open repository of genetic variant age estimations and an extensive catalog of single nucleotide changes distinguishing hominins, we uncover a coincidence between the establishment of globularity and the time of emergence of modifications in the cerebrospinal fluid proteome. Overall, we provide a finer-grained genetic architecture for globularity, with novel biological associations to traits across evolutionary and developmental timescales, leading us to draw implications for the early development of cognitive networks but also for liabilities to neurodegeneration late in life.

papers.title: Ancient Mitogenomes from Belize Provide Insights into the Mobility and Migration of Ancient Communities in Mesoamerica and the Caribbean.
papers.abstract: Maya peoples have undergone several largescale demographic transformations over the past 3000 years, including the formation and depopulation of large urban centers, climatic events, and multiple colonial regimes. Archaeological and stable isotope evidence from across the Maya lowlands throughout these periods paints a picture of a demographically mobile population with complex and dynamic relationships among some of the largest urban polities in antiquity. The nature of the genomic relationship between ancient Maya urban centers, as well as their relationship with present-day Maya communities, however, remains under-characterized. Here, we present mitogenomic data of 16 ancient Maya Ancestors recovered from interments in the ancient Maya cities of Caracol and Santa Rita Corozal located in Western and Northern Belize. These ancient data were combined with 110 newly collected contemporary individuals from Northern Belize, along with nearly 600 previously published ancient and contemporary comparative mitogenomes recovered from sites spanning Mesoamerica and the Caribbean to reconstruct paleodemographic and mobility patterns of maternal lineages through time. Our results are consistent with broadly interconnected Maya populations that have maintained maternal genetic continuity across much of the Holocene, and which are not structured by linguistic family.

papers.title: Placental cis-eQTL analysis identifies preeclampsia-dependent genetic regulation at promoters
papers.abstract: Background: Preeclampsia (PE) is a hypertensive pregnancy disorder with contributions from both maternal and fetal genetic factors, but how both genomes regulate placental transcription remains incompletely understood. Results: We analyzed placental 5'-end RNA sequencing data from 59 pregnancies in the FINNPEC cohort and performed separate maternal and fetal cis-eQTL analyses using gene-level expression and promoter-level expression defined as Transcript Far 5' Ends (TFE). Genotype-by-PE interaction models were used to identify genetic effects that differ according to PE status. No gene-level interaction eQTLs remained significant after multiple-testing correction, although suggestive signals included LILRB2 in the maternal and LPCAT3 in the fetal analyses. In contrast, we identified two significant syntenic promoter-level interaction eQTLs: rs12504642-TFE61820 at the FHDC1 locus in the maternal analysis and rs1557150-TFE9032 at the PPIAP31 locus in the fetal analysis. Conclusion: These findings suggest that PE-dependent genetic interaction effects may be detectable at specific transcript promoter regions even when they are not captured at annotated gene levels.

papers.title: QTL analysis of essential oil, seed shattering, thousand-grain weight and stalk attachment rate in Carum carvi
papers.abstract: Caraway (Carum carvi L., 2n = 2x = 20) is a medicinal and aromatic plant of the Apiaceae family valued for its essential oil with the major terpenoids carvone and limonene. While the essential oil content represents an important quality trait, low seed shattering and high thousand-grain weight (TGW) are key determinants of seed yield. As molecular tools remain scarce within Apiaceae breeding beyond carrot, we conducted a QTL mapping for these seed-related traits using two previously established F2 populations (Effective N(P1) = 236; N(P2) = 266). In P1 with the non-shattering maternal parent Rekord, QTL mapping revealed at least one shattering locus on LG03 (PVE: 9.9%). In addition, loci associated with essential oil (LG08, 10.5% PVE) and TGW (LG09, 11.1% PVE) were detected. In P2, we identified six essential-oil loci (LG02-06, LG10; combined PVE: 49.2%), with five loci affecting both carvone and limonene, and one (LG03) exclusively limonene. Additionally, a major QTL for TGW mapped to LG02 (PVE: 15.6%). For stalk attachment rate one minor QTL was detected (LG07, 8.5% PVE), while no QTL co-localized with the major shattering locus. To pave the path towards fine-mapping, we designed and validated 26 diagnostic PACE markers covering five key QTLs.

papers.title: Maternal repression of imprinted genes in endosperm by gene body demethylation
papers.abstract: Removal of TE-like DNA methylation from regulatory elements drives canonical genomic imprinting of both maternally and paternally expressed genes in endosperm (MEGs and PEGs). Here we report that removal of CG-only gene body methylation also drives imprinting in maize, resulting in maternally repressed PEGs. These CG body methylated PEGs express broadly across cell types and lack H3K27me3 except in endosperm, where maternal copies acquire it. We found that partial gene body demethylation is a widespread feature of endosperm genes, usually does not result in imprinted expression, and is mediated by DNA glycosylases/lyases (DNGs). These and other data indicate that gene body methylation can shield select genes from PRC2 repression, and its maternal removal by DNGs explains the majority of PEGs in maize and rice but has weak impact in Arabidopsis thaliana. We hypothesize that increased gene expression noise arising from gene body demethylation--both with and without imprinting--is beneficial in endosperm.

papers.title: Recent effective population size of the snowy owl (Bubo scandiacus) tracks historical climate variation
papers.abstract: Arctic ecosystems are undergoing rapid climate warming, providing an opportunity to examine molecular evolution under environmental stress. Here, we used whole-genome resequencing to assess population structure, genetic diversity, and recent demographic history in the snowy owl (Bubo scandiacus), a highly mobile Arctic apex predator classified as Vulnerable by the IUCN. We analysed genome-wide data from individuals sampled across the species' circumpolar range using a chromosome-level reference genome. Population genomic analyses revealed an absence of detectable population structure, indicating extensive gene flow and near-panmixia across continents. Genome-wide nucleotide diversity was low ({pi}= 2.47 x 10^(-4)), while runs of homozygosity were dominated by short tracts, indicating limited standing genetic variation despite little evidence for recent close inbreeding. Our demographic inference revealed a sustained decline in effective population size over the past ~1,600 years, a pronounced reduction coinciding with the Medieval Warm Period followed by a partial recovery during the subsequent cooler interval. This direct, measurable effect of past climate warming on effective population size raises concerns for the long-term survival of the snowy owl. Our results demonstrate that high connectivity and low levels of recent inbreeding have not necessarily buffered this species against climate-driven demographic erosion of genetic diversity. This study highlights the value of using whole-genome population genomics to inform genomic monitoring and conservation decision-making in rapidly changing environments.

papers.title: Inbred and outcrossed Drosophila embryos diverge in stress defense and developmental maintenance during heat stress
papers.abstract: Early embryos must mount stress defenses without compromising the developmental programs that drive morphogenesis, but whether genetic background alters this balance remains unclear. We compared cellularizing Drosophila melanogaster embryos from inbred and outcrossed backgrounds under control conditions and after acute or chronic heat-stress. Both backgrounds developed successfully and showed modest transcriptomic differences at 18{degrees}C. Heat stress at 32{degrees}C, however, sharply separated their phenotypic and transcriptional responses. Inbred embryos showed poor larval hatching after acute and chronic heat, and this deficit persisted through adult eclosion. Their transcriptomes exhibited a greater stress-response burden, with enrichment of proteostasis, DNA repair, mitochondrial maintenance, RNA processing, and metabolic remodeling programs. Outcrossed embryos retained substantially greater developmental survival and higher abundance of transcripts associated with development, adhesion, epithelial organization, signaling, transport, sensory responses, and morphogenesis. Background-dependent divergence was greatest during acute heat. Under chronic heat, background-dependent differences were fewer, with most overlapping those seen during acute heat and a smaller set detected only under chronic heat. Transcript-origin analysis further showed that acute outcrossed-biased genes were predominantly maternally derived and showed no enrichment for purely zygotic transcripts, whereas chronic outcrossed-biased genes contained a larger zygotic component. In summary, the less viable inbred background mounted the broader molecular stress signature, whereas the more viable outcrossed background retained greater abundance of development-associated transcripts. These findings identify genetic background as a major determinant of how embryonic heat responses are distributed between molecular stress defense and developmental gene expression.

papers.title: Linkage disequilibrium moderates how evolving genetic background shapes variant-level architecture
papers.abstract: Evolutionary theory offers a unifying explanation for the genetics of complex traits and diseases by modeling how a trait and its genetic basis are maintained by evolutionary forces. A growing body of evidence suggests that linkage disequilibrium (LD) couples a variant's evolution to that of the genetic background it resides on. However, widely used single-variant theories omit this coupling between variants and the background, or hold the background fixed. We close this gap by developing a model of linkage LD evolution accounting for stabilizing selection, recombination, and genetic drift. The model deduces the genetic architecture of individual variants subject to the co-evolving genetic background. More efficient selection in larger populations is partially offset by slower decay of existing LD and increased generation of new LD. Conversely, noisier LD in smaller populations exposes the variants to episodes of stronger selection. We ask whether ancestry differences in the relationship between effect-size magnitude and minor allele frequency require different selection strengths or can arise from differences in demographic history alone. Stabilizing selection needs to be more than three times stronger in Africans than in Europeans under the constant-size demography, whereas an Out-of-Africa demography alone can explain most of the observed frequency-dependence gap. As this example indicates, selection strength is in general not identifiable from the frequency--effect-size relationship alone, because different combinations of selection and demographic history can produce the same pattern in data with further redundancy added by LD.

papers.title: Genomic SEM reveals shared genetic architecture and expands locus discovery for locomotor activity in heterogeneous stock rats
papers.abstract: Locomotor response to a novel environment is a heritable, addiction-relevant behavioral phenotype in rodents. We characterized its genetic basis in 9,341 male and female heterogeneous stock (HS) rats from eight studies. Locomotor activity was heritable across studies, while pairwise genetic correlations were positive but variable, indicating shared yet nonidentical genetic influences. Given nonuniform genetic architecture, we compared three complementary approaches to locus discovery that analyzed SNP effects 1) on a pooled locomotor phenotype (MEGA), 2) across studies under a fixed-effect model (METAL), or 3) on a shared genetic factor (Genomic SEM). To ensure comparability, all three locus-discovery approaches were applied to a common subset of seven studies. Together, these approaches identified 38 loci, with both convergence and method-specific discovery across analyses. Genomic SEM identified 31 loci, compared to 8 for MEGA and 13 for METAL. To interpret the loci, we integrated brain molecular QTLs, predicted coding and splice consequences, and open-field locomotor phenotypes from knockouts of orthologous mouse genes. Our results highlighted established neurobehavioral candidates spanning locomotor and reward-related biology (Negr1 and Lmo4), serotonergic signaling (Htr1b), and GABAergic signaling (Gabrg2), as well as relatively novel genes including Tcerg1l, Pcdh10, and Tmem132e. Our results illustrate how Genomic SEM can integrate genetically correlated yet heterogeneous behavioral measures and enable discovery of loci underlying their shared genetic architecture, highlighting its utility for complex-trait studies in rodents.

papers.title: Selection on cuticle color produces a genome-wide response that does not localize to known major genes in Drosophila
papers.abstract: Complex traits are often deemed highly polygenic when a mapping study fails to localize the loci underlying them, but a result that fails to identify major genes can also reflect a lack of power. Cuticle color in Drosophila offers a natural test of this distinction, since genes of large effect segregate in natural populations. We selected for dark and light thoracic trident color for 16 generations in two populations of D. melanogaster and two of D. simulans, then used pooled sequencing to scan each genome for allele-frequency differentiation between selected and control lines. Selection produced a strong, genome-wide shift in allele frequencies in every population, exceeding the expectation under drift. Simulations demonstrate that our design has low power to detect major-effect genes, which may explain why we do not observe peaks localizing to known color genes. We further show that a highly significant peak in each genome, on chromosome 3L, is an artifact of chorion-gene amplification in the pooled adult females. A source of false signal in pool-seq studies that has not been reported before. Cosmopolitan inversions shifted in frequency under selection in the one population that carried them, but direct testing showed they did not inflate genome-wide noise, contradicting a common assumption in the field. Together, these results demonstrate that a diffuse, polygenic-type response can arise from a trait with known large-effect genes, and provide a quantitative account of why an evolve-and-resequence design can fail to localize even a well-characterized genetic architecture.

papers.title: A new mouse model for a high-risk AMD variant, ARMS2A69S
papers.abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of irreversible central vision loss in older adults. The highest genetic risk for AMD maps to Chromosome 10q26. However, due to strong linkage disequilibrium between two genes, ARMS2 and HTRA1 located in this region, it has been difficult to determine whether one or both genes contribute to the AMD-disease risk. Functional studies of ARMS2 have been hampered due to the lack of animal models, as orthologs are only found in the higher primates and the gene is absent in rodents. To model ARMS2 biology in vivo, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to insert the complete human ARMS2 gene carrying the A69S risk variant (rs10490924), into a region of homology between humans and mice, on mouse Chromosome 7, 3.5 kb upstream of Htra1, preserving its native promoter, spacing, and orientation. We also generated a mouse model bearing its wild-type counterpart ARMS2A69 (ARMS2WT). RNA analysis revealed tissue- and cell-type-specific pattern of ARMS2 expression enriched in neural tissues, testis, and eye, and within the eye, in retinal horizontal cells and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). ARMS2 expression was consistent with human expression data and unaltered by the A69S mutation. By 12 months, ARMS2A69S mice develop AMD-relevant phenotypes including increased fundus spots, A69S-specific thinning of the outer nuclear layer, and reduced scotopic ERG amplitudes. Transcriptomic profiling of postnatal day 14 retina and RPE-enriched fractions revealed reduced mitochondrial oxidative-phosphorylation genes, corroborated by reduced retinal mtDNA copy number and lower maximal respiration, alongside preliminary results that suggest sphingolipid remodeling in the RPE. This humanized model links the ARMS2 A69S variant to mitochondrial dysfunction and provides an in vivo platform for defining AMD mechanisms and testing therapies.

papers.title: Adaptive introgression in subdivided populations leaves distinct genomic footprints under global and local selection: a case study in Ciona intestinalis
papers.abstract: Adaptive introgression, the transfer of beneficial alleles between species through hybridization, is increasingly recognized as an important source of adaptation to novel environments. However, the theory of adaptive introgression has primarily been developed for a single panmictic population, whereas many empirical examples involve spatially subdivided populations. In such systems, a low-frequency adaptive allele may either represent the leading edge of an adaptive travelling wave or occur in a subpopulation where the introgressed allele is locally selected against. We developed a simple prediction based on the relationship between adaptive allele frequency and introgressed tract length. Simulations predict a positive correlation during an ongoing sweep of an unconditionally beneficial allele, but no correlation under local adaptation. Tract erosion provides a recombination clock for time since introgression, which also determines the distance travelled by the adaptive wave and hence allele frequency in the former, whereas allele frequency is determined by local selection in the latter. We tested this prediction in a well-characterized case of adaptive introgression, in the sea squirt Ciona intestinalis, using haplotagging to reconstruct phased genomes and local ancestry. We found no relationship between adaptive allele frequency and introgressed tract length, providing additional support for a model of local adaptation rather than ongoing global selective sweep.

papers.title: Developmental Convergence Across Diverse Genetic Architectures in Childhood Apraxia of Speech
papers.abstract: Childhood apraxia of speech (CAS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder of speech-motor planning and programming, associated with literacy, academic, and psychosocial difficulties. We performed whole-exome sequencing in 11 families comprising 21 affected and 15 unaffected individuals with phenotyping spanning speech, language, cognition, literacy, and motor function. We identified 60 prioritized variant observations representing 22 unique variants across 20 genes with family-based segregation analysis assessed in informative relatives; 5 arose de novo. Our cohort included multiple affected siblings and extended relatives, with several families carrying multiple prioritized variants, suggesting cumulative or oligogenic susceptibility. Speech and literacy impairment co-occurred with oral-motor, feeding, and fine-motor difficulties. BrainSpan co-expression analysis identified MECP2 and ANK2 as the genes with the highest observed connectivity in the sampled postnatal network. Exploratory analysis of the KOLF2.1J perturbation atlas in undifferentiated human induced pluripotent stem cells identified a positive LMO3 expression-response score following NIPBL repression and opposing LMO3 and ANK2 response directions within a cohesin-associated perturbation cluster. These observations motivate testing in human neural cells. Functional enrichment, protein-association, and developmental-expression analyses supported shared biological themes involving chromatin regulation, neuronal signaling, and extracellular-matrix organization. Among six families, multiple affected relatives shared prioritized variants across a unique set of several genes, demonstrating multilocus candidate profiles whose individual and combined effects may contribute to CAS susceptibility. We propose four novel CAS candidate genes: LMO3 and PCDH10, previously linked to human accelerated regions, as well as MYCBP2 and PTPRS. Our work provides multiple testable hypotheses for future variant-specific functional validation in speech-motor development.

papers.title: Significance filtering induces denominator selection bias in local genetic correlation: closed-form characterisation, a gate-aware correction, and an applicability diagnostic
papers.abstract: Local genetic correlation is estimated as a ratio of a local genetic covariance to the geometric mean of two local heritabilities. LAVA, the standard implementation, returns that ratio only where both traits clear a univariate heritability test at P < 0.05, a rule its documentation presents as a stabiliser. We show that it is a selection event acting on the denominator, and characterise what it does to the estimates that survive. Under the noncentral Wishart model LAVA's own interval routine assumes, the gate-conditional mean of the estimator is affine in the true correlation, with slope and intercept available in closed form from quantities every run already reports, that is, the components retained, the two univariate P-values, and the sample-overlap correlation. Attenuation is therefore a property of the analysis, not of the method. Across six psychiatric trait pairs the measured slope runs from 0.579 to 0.923 and the closed form predicts each to within 0.007 with nothing fitted to the panel, while within a single pair it runs from 0.371 to 0.971, so no single factor can correct it. Overlap and the filter jointly manufacture correlation where the truth is zero, most where power is lowest. We invert the closed form into a gate-aware correction, which reduces mean absolute bias from 0.247 to 0.026 over 48 simulation cells, and pair it with a diagnostic that decides whether the correction is identified. Three pairs fail it, all three sharing one trait whose local heritabilities are indistinguishable from a complete local null.

papers.title: Voluntary Exercise Differentially Affects High-Fat Induced Metabolic Phenotypes Across BXD Mouse Strains
papers.abstract: Obesity and metabolic diseases such as diabetes reflect long-term interactions between diet, lifestyle, and genetics, variables that are hard to control in humans but can be systematically varied in mice, though behavioral variables like long-term exercise remain harder to model. Having previously phenotyped ~50 BXD strains, we identified BXD40, BXD43, and BXD100 as predisposed to voluntary wheel-running (~6 km/day at 24 weeks) with variable susceptibility to diet-induced obesity and diabetes. We followed these strains from 8-32 weeks on a 60% kcal/fat high-fat (HF) diet, with or without access to running wheels. Wheel usage declined from ~9 km/day in the first two weeks to a steady ~5 km/day thereafter yet still improved oral glucose tolerance by 35% over sedentary controls by 24 weeks. Despite equivalent body weight, runners ate 20% more relative to body weight, indicating the glucose benefit was independent of caloric intake. We next asked whether the gut microbiome contributes to this benefit. Long-term exercise produced only modest, cohort-dependent shifts in cecal microbial composition, though functional profiling revealed exercise-associated differences in carbohydrate- and glucose-metabolism pathways. Reciprocal bedding exchange between sedentary and running BXD43 cages reduced microbial differentiation in a taxon-specific manner and coincided with marked attenuation of the glucose phenotype, despite unchanged running behavior. Together, these findings validate BXD40, BXD43, and BXD100, alongside the canonical C57BL/6, as a model for studying diet, exercise, and genetics in metabolic disease, and implicate gut microbial taxa in shaping exercise's metabolic effects during HF feeding.

papers.title: GWAS of flag leaf primary metabolites uncovers metabolic QTL hubs linked to grain yield stability under drought in field-grown indica rice
papers.abstract: Reproductive stage drought disrupts flag leaf metabolism in rice (Oryza sativa), limiting photoassimilate translocation to developing grains and reducing grain yield (GY). How natural variation in this response relates to GY remains poorly understood. This study combines untargeted metabolomics of flag leaves from 271 indica rice accessions grown under well-watered (WW) and reproductive-stage water-limited (WL) field conditions with genome-wide association studies of 89 annotated polar metabolites. A total of 180 metabolite quantitative trait loci (mQTLs) were identified: 93 detected only under WL, 68 only under WW, and 19 under both conditions, indicating a predominant stress-dependent genetic control; mapping of GY itself detected only four marginal QTLs, none overlapping the mQTLs. Four high-density regions (HDRs) of mQTLs were identified: HDR1-1, detected only under WW conditions and associated mainly with raffinose family oligosaccharides; HDR1-2, HDR4, and HDR11, detected only under WL conditions and associated mainly with tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates and amino acids. After correcting for genetic relatedness, accessions carrying the favourable haplotype at both HDR1-2 and HDR4 yielded 21.5% more under WL conditions than accessions carrying the unfavourable haplotype at both loci and lost 11.4 percentage points less GY to stress. Accessions carrying the favourable haplotype at only one locus showed a comparable reduction in yield loss. Haplotype-guided variant detection against the 3,000 Rice Genomes Project panel identified major-impact variants in candidate genes, including a polyphenol oxidase at HDR1-2 and tandem cytochrome P450s at HDR4. These hubs are promising, metabolically defined targets for breeding drought-resilient rice.

papers.title: Mutation choice biases the structure of empirical fitness landscapes
papers.abstract: Evolution can be thought of as taking place in a fitness landscape which maps each genotype to a fitness value. This abstraction has motivated significant efforts to quantify the statistical properties of random fitness landscapes with different amounts and types of interactions among loci---broadly referred to as epistasis. New high-throughput experimental techniques measuring the phenotypes of thousands of genotypes promise to bridge this theory with data. Yet, while impressive, thousands is still small relative to the size of genotype space. Moreover, experiments often assay a highly non-random subset of the fitness landscape. For example, a common experimental approach is to generate all possible 2M sequence intermediates between ancestral and evolved sequences differing by M much less than L mutations. Here, we ask to what extent the statistics of an empirical landscape constructed under distinct ascertainment protocols recapitulate the statistics of a random subset of the global landscape in a few well-studied random landscape models. We show that, in most landscapes, selecting mutations which occurred along an adaptive trajectory inflates the variance explained by lower order epistasis, reduces the number of local maxima, and increases the number of accessible paths relative to a random fitness landscape. Selecting the most beneficial or deleterious mutations, on the other hand, results in distortions to these statistics which depend more critically on the amount of epistasis in the global landscape. We then take advantage of several large-scale mutagenesis datasets to simulate the effects of ascertainment in more realistic settings.

papers.title: The effects of hitchhiking and repulsion of deleterious alleles on linkage disequilibrium during a selective sweep
papers.abstract: Deleterious mutations are abundant in nature. Consequently, when an adaptive mutation arises, it will likely land on a haplotype with several deleterious mutations. While deleterious mutations may hitchhike with the adaptive variant, deleterious mutations are less likely to be found on the same haplotype with each other due to repulsion (i.e. Hill Robertson interference). Both hitchhiking and repulsion shape patterns of linkage disequilibrium (LD), but their simultaneous impact on LD have not been fully understood, leaving a gap in accurate inference of selection from genomic data. Here, we investigate patterns of LD during a sweep using simulations across a wide range of evolutionary parameters. On average, LD is elevated between pairs of intermediate frequency nonsynonymous variants relative to synonymous variants. This occurs because nonsynonymous variants, which are presumably deleterious, are more likely to rise to high frequency via hitchhiking rather than drift and thus will be predominantly found on the sweeping haplotype. However, we find that this elevation does not occur across all distances: when nonsynonymous variants are either too close to each other or too far from the adaptive locus, repulsion between deleterious variants results in lower LD among nonsynonymous variants. This results in a characteristic "criss-crossing" of LD. We find that criss-crossing is a feature of empirical data from Clostridioides difficile, a pathogen that has undergone several selective sweeps. However, some sweeps show elevation of nonsynonymous LD over synonymous LD across all distances. These sweeps have been previously identified to bear complex adaptations, and moreover, harbor elevated nucleotide diversity. Consistent with this, we demonstrate that lack of criss-crossing can arise when adaptation proceeds via epistatic, multi-locus architecture or introgression.

papers.title: The ortholog of the Human T2D Risk Gene STEAP2 is Required for Glucose Stimulated Insulin Secretion in Mice
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes is a complex metabolic disease with a strong genetic component, yet this genetic risk is driven by common variants in up to 600 loci with small effect sizes. Variants in the STEAP2 locus, encoding Six-transmembrane epithelial antigen of the prostate-2, are highly associated with altered glycemic traits and type 2 diabetes risk. To elucidate its function in pancreatic beta-cells, we utilized Crisp-Cas9 assisted homologous recombination to derive a conditional null allele for Steap2 (Steap2fl/fl) in mice and crossed this to the rat insulin promoter (Rip)-Cre transgene. Ablation of Steap2 induced glucose intolerance, blunted glucose-stimulated Ca2+ mobilization and stunted first phase glucose-simulated insulin secretion. In contrast, the incretin effect and second phase insulin secretion were not affected. Islet respirometry and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) identified disrupted cristate morphology and impaired glucose-stimulated oxygen consumption as causally responsible for the observed, impaired triggering pathway of insulin secretion. These findings suggest that at least part of the genetic risk for T2D conferred by Steap2 variants is likely due to its function in maintaining optimal mitochondrial respiration in pancreatic beta-cells.

papers.title: Genetic backgrounds and sex modulate indirect genetic effects of Epha4 in laboratory mice
papers.abstract: The phenotype of a focal individual can be affected not only by the individuals own genes (direct genetic effects, DGE) but also by genes of other individuals it interacts with (indirect genetic effects, IGE). Better understanding IGE can help better understand the impact and mechanisms of social effects. Here, we investigated, in laboratory mice, the modulation of IGE by genetic background of the focal individual (social epistasis) and by sex. We focused on IGE arising from Epha4, a gene that has been associated with the individuals own stress-related and social behaviours (i.e. DGE) and the stress-coping behaviour and wound healing of the other mice in the cage (i.e. IGE). Among four different genetic backgrounds for focal mice, significant IGE from Epha4 were detected in CBA females only. A formal model selection analysis was consistent with the modulation of IGE by the similarity of the genetic backgrounds of the focal mouse and its Epha4 cage mate, as well as by sex. Observations of fighting in cages of males with dissimilar genetic backgrounds suggested aggression might underpin these modulatory effects, which prompted to us to expand the conceptual framework describing the mechanisms of social epistasis. Thus, our results strengthen the emerging view that IGE are not fixed properties of social genotypes but can depend on the genetic and sex context of interacting individuals, revealing an underexplored layer of their genetic architecture.

papers.title: Finding dugongs through environmental DNA: a complementary tool for population surveillance
papers.abstract: Detecting dugongs at low densities remains a major challenge for conservation monitoring, particularly in remote or turbid coastal habitats where conventional surveys are difficult. Environmental DNA (eDNA) offers a complementary approach, but robust species-specific tools are needed before it can be confidently applied to dugong surveillance. We developed and analytically validated a quantitative PCR TaqMan assay for detecting dugong (Dugong dugon) eDNA and evaluated its performance across controlled aquarium conditions in Australia and Abu Dhabi, and wild populations in northern Australia and the Arabian/Persian Gulf. The assay detected dugong eDNA in aquarium and field samples, with Sanger sequencing confirming amplification of dugong mitochondrial DNA from positive field detections. Our assay provides a robust and geographically transferable tool for targeted dugong eDNA detection, performing reliably across contrasting coastal environments and widely separated populations. This approach can strengthen local-scale surveillance of low-density or difficult-to-detect dugong populations.

papers.title: Multi-omics fine-mapping uncovers a pleiotropic intestinal enhancer variant linking PMAIP1 regulation to pig growth and fatness
papers.abstract: Genetic loci influencing multiple complex traits often remain difficult to interpret because the underlying functional variants, target genes and tissue contexts are unresolved. Here, we investigated the regulatory basis of a shared signal for average daily gain (ADG) and backfat thickness (BF) in Yorkshire pigs. By integrating GWAS in 7,972 pigs, targeted capture sequencing, LD-based fine-mapping, porcine epigenomic annotations, three-dimensional chromatin interaction maps and functional assays, we narrowed the shared SSC1 signal to a 1.59-Mb interval and functionally prioritized rs334769214 (T>G) as the leading candidate variant. The T>G substitution produced marked allele-specific differences in enhancer activity and nuclear-protein binding, while transcription-factor co-transfection assays identified FOXL1-responsive, allele-dependent regulatory activity. Chromatin interaction and CRISPRa analyses supported a regulatory connection between the rs334769214-containing enhancer and PMAIP1, and PMAIP1 overexpression promoted apoptosis in porcine intestinal epithelial cells. In the capture-sequenced subset, the G allele was associated with higher ADG and BF, consistent with a relative loss-of-activation model. Together, these findings delineate a candidate FOXL1-enhancer-PMAIP1 regulatory pathway and demonstrate how multi-omics fine-mapping can advance a shared quantitative-trait locus toward a testable molecular mechanism underlying variation in growth and fatness.

papers.title: Fluorescent Ubiquitination-based Trbl Turnover Indicator (FUTTI): A tool to detect activity of the Tribbles pseudokinase in vivo
papers.abstract: Targeted protein turnover of the transcription factor C/EBP is enhanced by the Tribbles (Trib) pseudokinase family of adaptor proteins, which bind to a conserved degron motif in C/EBP substrate and recruit a cognate COP1 E3 ligase to ubiquitinate C/EBP for degradation. We identified a conserved degron in the Drosophila C/EBP ortholog Slbo and fused this motif to a fluorescent protein (GFP or RFP) under the control of a constitutive promoter. Transgenic flies expressing this fluorescent protein (FP)::degron transgene, which we call the Fluorescent Ubiquitination-based Trbl Turnover Indicator (or FUTTI) sensor, showed reduced levels of fluorescence in response to increased levels of Drosophila Tribbles (Trbl) and conversely, increased levels when Trbl activity was reduced. Mutations in the Trbl conserved pseudokinase substrate binding pocket and in a divergent PEST-like motif in the C-terminal tail region disrupted Trbl activity in the FUTTI assay. These data indicate that FUTTI will be a valuable tool to identify sites of Trbl activity in vivo and the critical features of the protein required for function.

papers.title: A genetic screen to identify novel interactions of the phosphatidylinositol phosphate signaling pathway in Drosophila spermatogenesis
papers.abstract: Phosphatidylinositol (PI) phosphates (PIPs) are membrane lipids with crucial roles in intracellular signaling, membrane trafficking and cytoskeletal organization. To perturb PIP function in Drosophila melanogaster sperm development, we previously expressed the Salmonella PIP phosphatase SigD (also known as SopB) under control of a spermatocyte- specific promoter. SigD expression results in reduced levels of plasma membrane PI 4,5-bisphosphate [PI(4,5)P2; henceforth PIP2] and male sterility. Transgenic lines expressing high levels of SigD (SigD-high) exhibit defects in spermatocyte cytokinesis, ciliary transition zone maturation and spermatid elongation, whereas lines expressing low levels of SigD (SigD-low) have defects in nuclear shaping and spermatid cell polarization. To further investigate the role of PIPs during Drosophila sperm development, we conducted a sensitized genetic screen to identify suppressors and enhancers of SigD-low phenotypes. From a screen of 760 chromosomal deficiencies spanning 83.6% of chromosomes 2 and 3, we identified 80 interacting regions that were further narrowed down to 40 individual suppressors. Among the strongest interactors were genes involved in microtubule dynamics, nucleocytoplasmic transport and membrane trafficking. The novel genetic interactions identified by our screen pave the way for further investigation into molecular mechanisms underlying the affected aspects of sperm development.

papers.title: TET loss of function selects for aneuploidies that confer a proliferative advantage
papers.abstract: Mutations in the Ten-Eleven Translocation (TET) family of DNA dioxygenases are among the most common epigenetic alterations in clonal hematopoiesis and hematologic malignancies, yet how TET loss of function reshapes genome evolution during cellular expansion remains to be fully understood. Here we show that loss of Tet2/3 in invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells drives aggressive lymphoid expansion that is consistently associated with recurrent chromosome 17 trisomy, a dominant aneuploid state observed across more than ten independently derived tumors following transplantation into immunocompetent recipient mice. Single-cell whole-genome sequencing of TET-deficient iNKT cells induced to proliferate in culture with antigen and IL-2 stimulation revealed that rare pre-existing cells with chromosome 17 trisomy appeared soon after Tet gene deletion in the thymus, together with cells harboring other copy number alterations, but only the cells with chromosome 17 trisomy were progressively enriched during further expansion. Similarly, inducibly Tet-deficient mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) showed selection for aneuploid states that were present prior to Tet gene deletion, including trisomy of chromosome 6. Reanalysis of independent datasets from Dnmt3a-deficient mouse lymphomas identified recurrent chromosome gains, including chromosome 17 trisomy. Our results establish TET and DNMT3A deficiency as drivers of karyotypic evolution, and suggest that disruption of DNA methylation/ demethylation pathways through either TET or DNMT3A deletion promotes chromosomal instability, in part by facilitating the emergence and selection of cryptic aneuploid subclones during clonal expansion.
